[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#core-principles]

### Core Principles

The following principles guide AI data security and privacy architecture at Gainwell, extending enterprise data security principles (GUID-SEC-DATA-REF-1.5.01) to address AI-specific risks.
page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#principle-1-privacy-by-design-throughout-the-ai-data-lifecycle]

#### Principle 1: Privacy-by-Design Throughout the AI Data Lifecycle

**Description**: Privacy must be embedded from the earliest stages of AI data collection and curation, not bolted on later. Every phase of the AI data lifecycle—collection, storage, preparation, training, inference, and retention—must incorporate privacy controls appropriate to the data sensitivity and AI use case.

**Rationale**: Privacy vulnerabilities introduced early in the AI data lifecycle (e.g., unnecessary PHI retention, overly broad consent) are difficult to remediate later. Models trained on improperly handled data inherit privacy risks. Privacy-by-design ensures compliance and minimizes re-work.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL enforce data minimization, retaining only the data elements necessary for the documented AI use case
- The capability SHALL enforce purpose limitation, binding AI training datasets to documented permitted uses and prohibiting secondary use without explicit authorization
- The capability SHALL require a completed privacy impact assessment before AI data collection or processing begins for any system handling PHI or PII
- The capability SHALL apply de-identification or pseudonymization at the earliest feasible point in the AI data pipeline, isolating identifiable data from training workflows
- The capability SHOULD surface consent status for AI/ML processing at the point of data ingestion and enforce documented opt-outs across all pipelines

**Reference**: NIST Privacy Framework Core Function "Identify-P" (develop understanding of privacy risks); HIPAA Privacy Rule minimum necessary standard (45 CFR 164.502(b)); NIST AI RMF "Data Privacy" characteristic.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#principle-2-defense-in-depth-for-ai-training-data]

#### Principle 2: Defense-in-Depth for AI Training Data

**Description**: Protect AI training data through multiple, layered security controls that address different threat vectors. No single control is sufficient; assume attackers may bypass one layer and ensure others remain effective.

**Rationale**: AI training datasets are high-value targets (concentrated PHI, intellectual property). Breaches have occurred through misconfigured cloud storage, credential theft, insider threats, and supply chain compromises. Defense-in-depth reduces risk of catastrophic data exposure.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL protect AI training data at rest and in transit using current enterprise-approved cryptographic standards, with encryption key management under centralized, access-controlled key management services
- The capability SHALL enforce role-based and attribute-based access controls, limiting training data access to authorized individuals scoped to specific AI projects and roles
- The capability SHALL store AI training data in isolated network zones with restricted ingress and egress, preventing direct exposure to internet-accessible systems
- The capability SHALL apply automated data loss prevention policies to AI training data stores and pipelines, detecting and blocking unauthorized exfiltration
- The capability SHALL maintain comprehensive, tamper-evident audit logs of all access to AI training data, capturing who accessed what, when, and for what purpose
- The capability SHOULD apply dynamic data masking for non-production and exploratory access, protecting sensitive fields outside of controlled training contexts

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 controls SC-8 (transmission confidentiality), SC-28 (protection of information at rest), AC-3 (access enforcement); NIST AI RMF "Secure and Resilient" characteristic.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#principle-3-de-identification-and-anonymization-appropriate-for-ai]

#### Principle 3: De-identification and Anonymization Appropriate for AI

**Description**: Traditional de-identification (removing direct identifiers per HIPAA Safe Harbor) may be insufficient for AI. Apply enhanced de-identification techniques that account for linkage attacks, quasi-identifier re-identification, and model-based inference risks.

**Rationale**: AI models can infer sensitive attributes from non-obvious features. Studies show that removing names/SSNs but retaining demographics, diagnoses, and dates enables re-identification through linkage attacks. Quasi-identifiers (age, ZIP code, dates) combined with external datasets can uniquely identify individuals. AI-aware de-identification is essential for privacy.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL apply de-identification methods that account for AI-specific re-identification risks, including quasi-identifier linkage and model-based inference, beyond traditional Safe Harbor identifier removal
- The capability SHALL conduct and document re-identification risk assessments before de-identified datasets are approved for AI training use, with statistical thresholds determined through a risk-based assessment appropriate to the dataset and use case
- The capability SHALL satisfy HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification requirements as a minimum baseline, augmented by statistical analysis commensurate with the sensitivity and intended AI application
- The capability SHOULD generalize quasi-identifiers (e.g., age ranges, geographic aggregation) and suppress rare values to reduce outlier-based re-identification risk
- The capability SHOULD engage qualified statistical expertise for re-identification risk evaluation on high-value, complex, or high-sensitivity datasets
- The capability SHALL assess linkage risk against known external and organizational datasets before approving de-identified data for AI training use

**Reference**: HIPAA Privacy Rule 45 CFR 164.514(b) (de-identification methods); NIST SP 800-188 (de-identifying government datasets); Article 29 Working Party Opinion 05/2014 (anonymization techniques).

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#principle-4-privacy-preserving-machine-learning-ppml-where-appropriate]

#### Principle 4: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML) Where Appropriate

**Description**: When data sensitivity or regulatory constraints preclude traditional centralized training, employ privacy-preserving ML techniques (differential privacy, federated learning, secure multi-party computation, synthetic data) to enable AI innovation without compromising privacy.

**Rationale**: Some use cases require training on data that cannot be centralized or accessed directly due to privacy/regulatory concerns. Privacy-preserving techniques provide mathematical or architectural guarantees that prevent individual privacy breaches while enabling model training. These techniques unlock AI opportunities otherwise blocked by privacy constraints.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL support differential privacy techniques for AI model training when data sensitivity or regulatory constraints require provable privacy guarantees; privacy budget parameters SHALL be documented with explicit justification based on data sensitivity, use case, and current authoritative guidance
- The capability SHOULD support federated learning or equivalent privacy-preserving distributed training where data cannot be centralized due to regulatory constraints, contractual limitations, or organizational boundaries
- The capability SHOULD support synthetic data generation as a privacy-safe alternative for model development, testing, and data sharing with third parties; generated datasets SHALL be validated to confirm they do not memorize or leak real records
- The capability MAY support secure multi-party computation where joint computation on sensitive data from multiple parties is required and no single party should have visibility into all inputs
- The capability MAY support trusted execution environments or equivalent hardware-isolated processing where in-memory data protection is required

**Reference**: NIST Privacy Framework "Disassociate-P" (enable processing while reducing data linkability); NIST AI RMF 1.0 "Data Privacy" characteristic; IEEE 7002-2022 (data privacy process standard).

---

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#principle-5-data-governance-and-accountability-for-ai]

#### Principle 5: Data Governance and Accountability for AI

**Description**: Establish clear governance structures, roles, and accountability for AI data security and privacy. Governance ensures consistent application of policies, provides oversight, and enables continuous improvement.

**Rationale**: Without governance, AI data privacy becomes ad-hoc and inconsistent. Governance assigns ownership, establishes reviews and approvals, defines metrics, and provides escalation paths for privacy issues. It bridges technical controls and organizational accountability.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL maintain a centralized, governed inventory of all AI training datasets, capturing source lineage, sensitivity classification, de-identification status, permitted purpose, retention policy, and current access controls
- The capability SHALL assign accountable data stewards for AI training datasets, responsible for classification, access reviews, lineage documentation, and compliance monitoring
- The capability SHALL require a mandatory privacy impact assessment for all AI projects processing PHI or PII, covering AI-specific risks including model inference and data aggregation
- The capability SHALL require data use agreements for all AI projects accessing PHI-derived training data, specifying permitted purposes, security obligations, and retention limits
- The capability SHALL produce and report privacy metrics sufficient to demonstrate ongoing compliance and governance effectiveness to appropriate oversight bodies
- The capability SHOULD establish cross-functional oversight of AI data privacy practices with authority to approve high-risk AI data uses and resolve policy questions

**Reference**: NIST Privacy Framework "Govern-P" function (accountability, risk management); NIST AI RMF "Govern" function (AI risk management); HIPAA Privacy Rule administrative requirements.

---
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#principle-6-transparency-and-individual-rights]

#### Principle 6: Transparency and Individual Rights

**Description**: Be transparent about AI data collection, use, and privacy practices. Honor individual rights (access, correction, deletion) even in the context of AI systems where implementation is complex.

**Rationale**: HIPAA and ethical AI principles require transparency and respect for individual rights. Patients have the right to know how their data is used, to access their data, and to request deletion. AI systems must accommodate these rights despite technical challenges (e.g., removing a record from a trained model may require retraining).

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL disclose AI/ML uses of PHI in privacy notices and consent documentation, providing plain-language examples of AI applications and their data uses
- The capability SHALL maintain processes to honor HIPAA individual rights — including access, amendment, and accounting of disclosures — in the context of AI data processing and AI-generated inferences
- The capability SHALL implement technically and procedurally sound approaches for honoring deletion requests that account for downstream impacts on trained models, including prevention of deleted records from future training and documented treatment of already-trained models
- The capability SHOULD provide meaningful explanations for high-stakes AI decisions that affect individual benefit eligibility, care recommendations, or other consequential determinations
- The capability SHOULD provide opt-out mechanisms for AI uses not required for core service delivery, and SHALL honor documented opt-outs across all data pipelines

**Reference**: HIPAA Privacy Rule individual rights (45 CFR 164.524, 164.526, 164.528); NIST AI RMF "Transparent and Explainable" characteristic; GDPR Articles 13-22 (information, access, erasure, explanation rights as ethical model).

---
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#principle-7-continuous-monitoring-for-privacy-threats]

#### Principle 7: Continuous Monitoring for Privacy Threats

**Description**: Actively monitor AI systems and data pipelines for privacy risks, including unauthorized data access, model-based privacy leakage, and privacy policy violations. Respond rapidly to privacy incidents.

**Rationale**: Privacy threats to AI systems evolve, and adversaries continuously develop new attack techniques (e.g., new membership inference methods). Passive compliance is insufficient; active monitoring detects anomalies, identifies policy violations, and enables rapid response to privacy incidents before significant harm occurs.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL continuously monitor AI training data stores for anomalous access patterns and alert on suspicious activity, including unusual access volumes, unexpected access locations, and access outside authorized time windows
- The capability SHALL periodically test deployed AI models for privacy leakage using recognized attack methodologies, including membership inference, model inversion, and attribute inference; results SHALL be evaluated against documented acceptable thresholds
- The capability SHALL detect and alert on large-scale or unauthorized data transfers from AI training data stores and integrate detection capabilities with enterprise data loss prevention and security operations
- The capability SHALL automate detection of violations of data use agreements, access policies, or retention policies and alert appropriate governance stakeholders
- The capability SHALL maintain and execute tailored incident response procedures for AI-specific privacy incidents, with defined roles for legal, privacy, and AI team participation in response

**Reference**: NIST CSF 2.0 "Detect" function (anomalies and events, security continuous monitoring); NIST AI RMF "Map" function (continuous monitoring of AI risks); HIPAA Security Rule 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (information system activity review).

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#hipaa-privacy-and-security-rules]

#### HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules

| **HIPAA Requirement** | **AI Data Privacy Control** | **Implementation** |
|-------------------|-------------------------|----------------|
| **Minimum Necessary (164.502(b))** | Data minimization for AI training | Collect only data elements required for AI use case; document necessity |
| **Uses and Disclosures (164.506)** | Purpose limitation and consent | Tag training data with permitted purposes; verify AI use is covered by consent/authorization |
| **De-Identification (164.514)** | Safe Harbor and Expert Determination | Apply 18-identifier removal or statistical de-identification; validate with k-anonymity |
| **Individual Access (164.524)** | Right to access AI-derived insights | Procedures to provide copies of AI-generated predictions/classifications about individual |
| **Amendment (164.526)** | Data correction in AI context | Process to correct errors in training data; assess impact on trained models |
| **Accounting of Disclosures (164.528)** | Logging of data access and sharing | Audit logs of training data access; tracking of model sharing with third parties |
| **Administrative Safeguards (164.308)** | Data governance and policies | AI Data Governance Oversight, PIAs, DUAs, training, access reviews |
| **Physical Safeguards (164.310)** | Secure data storage | Encrypted data lakes, physical security of on-prem AI infrastructure |
| **Technical Safeguards (164.312)** | Encryption, access controls, audit logs | AES-256 encryption, RBAC/ABAC, comprehensive audit logging, transmission security (TLS) |

#### NIST Privacy Framework

| **Privacy Framework Function** | **AI Data Privacy Activity** | **Outcome** |
|----------------------------|-------------------------|---------|
| **Identify-P** | Privacy risk assessments for AI projects | Documented AI-specific privacy risks (model leakage, re-identification) |
| **Govern-P** | AI Data Governance Oversight and policies | Accountability, roles, oversight for AI data privacy |
| **Control-P** | De-identification, access controls, DP | Technical and policy controls minimizing privacy risk |
| **Communicate-P** | Privacy notices, transparency about AI use | Members informed about AI processing of their data |
| **Protect-P** | Encryption, network segmentation, monitoring | Data protected throughout lifecycle against unauthorized access |
page_texts.21:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#nist-ai-risk-management-framework-ai-rmf-10]

#### NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

| **AI RMF Characteristic** | **AI Data Privacy Alignment** | **Evidence** |
|-----------------------|---------------------------|----------|
| **Valid and Reliable - Data Quality** | Data quality checks during curation | Training data validated for completeness, accuracy |
| **Safe - Prevent Privacy Harms** | De-identification, DP, monitoring | Privacy-preserving techniques reduce risk of privacy breaches |
| **Secure and Resilient - Data Security** | Encryption, access controls, DLP | Defense-in-depth protects training data from breaches |
| **Accountable and Transparent - Data Provenance** | Lineage tracking, PIAs | Data sources, transformations, and purposes documented |
| **Explainable - Data Transparency** | Data catalog, privacy notices | Stakeholders can understand what data is used in AI and why |
| **Privacy-Enhanced** | Core focus of this entire capability | All controls directly support privacy |

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-DATA-2.9.01.md#gdpr-principles-as-ethical-model-for-us-healthcare]

#### GDPR Principles (as Ethical Model for U.S. Healthcare)

While GDPR does not directly apply to most U.S. healthcare data, its principles inform privacy best practices:

| **GDPR Principle** | **Application to AI Data Privacy** | **Gainwell Implementation** |
|----------------|--------------------------------|-------------------------|
| **Lawfulness, Fairness, Transparency** | Clear legal basis and transparency for AI data use | Privacy notices disclose AI uses; consent documented |
| **Purpose Limitation** | Data collected for specific AI purpose only | Purpose tags on datasets; DUAs specify permitted uses |
| **Data Minimization** | Collect minimum data necessary | Data minimization policies; challenge data requests |
| **Accuracy** | Maintain accurate training data | Data quality processes; individual correction rights |
| **Storage Limitation** | Retention limits on training data | Automated retention policies; deletion after project or 7 years |
| **Integrity and Confidentiality** | Secure and confidential data processing | Encryption, access controls, audit logging |
| **Accountability** | Demonstrate compliance | PIAs, audit logs, governance committee oversight |
